sectionTitle: Permanent and induced magnetism, magnetic forces and fields

specStatements.text: The poles of a magnet are the places where the magnetic forces are strongest. When two magnets are brought close together they exert a force on each other. Two like poles repel each other. Two unlike poles attract each other. Attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact force.

A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field. An induced magnet is a material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field. Induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction. When removed from the magnetic field an induced magnet loses most/all of its magnetism quickly.
Students should be able to describe:
• the attraction and repulsion between unlike and like poles for permanent magnets
• the difference between permanent and induced magnets.
The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material (iron, steel, cobalt and nickel) is called the magnetic field.
The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction.
The strength of the magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet. The field is strongest at the poles of the magnet.

The direction of the magnetic field at any point is given by the direction of the force that would act on another north pole placed at that point. The direction of a magnetic field line is from the north (seeking) pole of a magnet to the south(seeking) pole of the magnet.
A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet. The Earth has a magnetic field. The compass needle points in the direction of the Earth’s magnetic field.
• describe how to plot the magnetic field pattern of a magnet using a compass
• draw the magnetic field pattern of a bar magnet showing how strength and direction change from one point to another
• explain how the behaviour of a magnetic compass is related to evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic.

scopeNotes.statement: a magnetic material (iron, steel, cobalt and nickel)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification names exactly four magnetic materials, and nothing here goes beyond that list. Questions that ask which materials a magnet attracts use only iron, steel, cobalt and nickel as the magnetic options, with common non-magnetic metals (copper, aluminium, brass, tin) as the contrast. No explanation of why these materials are magnetic is offered — magnetic domains, alloy composition and rare-earth magnets are not part of 4.7.1 and are not introduced.

concepts.definition: The poles of a magnet are the places where the magnetic forces are strongest. A bar magnet has two, a north (seeking) pole and a south (seeking) pole, one at each end.
Two like poles (north and north, or south and south) repel each other. Two unlike poles (north and south) attract each other. This rule applies to the poles of permanent magnets.

A force that acts between two objects that are not touching. The attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact force: the magnets push or pull on each other across a gap.
A magnet that produces its own magnetic field. It does not need another magnet nearby, and it keeps its field when it is moved away from other magnets.

A material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field. Induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction. When removed from the magnetic field an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly.
The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material. The field is there whether or not anything is placed in it, and whether or not any lines have been drawn.

A material on which a magnet's field exerts a force: iron, steel, cobalt and nickel. The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction, whichever pole of the magnet is used.
The strength of the magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet: the further away, the weaker the field. The field is strongest at the poles of the magnet.
The direction of the magnetic field at any point is given by the direction of the force that would act on another north pole placed at that point.
A line drawn to show the shape and direction of a magnetic field. The direction of a magnetic field line is from the north (seeking) pole of a magnet to the south (seeking) pole of the magnet.

An instrument that contains a small bar magnet, free to turn. The compass needle points in the direction of the magnetic field it sits in, so it can be used to find the direction of a field at a point.

The Earth has a magnetic field. Away from other magnets, a compass needle points in the direction of the Earth's magnetic field, which is why a compass can be used to find direction anywhere on the Earth's surface.

concepts.term: Plotting a field pattern with a compass
concepts.definition: Place the magnet on paper and draw round it. Put a plotting compass near one pole and mark a dot at each end of the needle. Move the compass so the tail of the needle sits on the last dot and mark again, repeating across the paper. Join the dots into a smooth curve and add an arrow showing the direction the needle pointed. Start again from other points to build up the whole pattern.

concepts.term: Field pattern of a bar magnet
concepts.definition: Smooth curved lines that leave the north pole, loop round outside the magnet and enter the south pole, each carrying an arrow from north to south. The lines are closest together at the poles, where the field is strongest, and spread further apart with distance, where the field is weaker.

concepts.term: Evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic
concepts.definition: A compass needle is itself a small magnet, so it lines up with the magnetic field it is in. Away from any other magnet, and anywhere on the Earth, it still settles in a definite direction. The field turning it must therefore be produced by the Earth itself, which is evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic.

misconceptions.question: Do two magnets always pull towards each other?
misconceptions.correct: No. Two like poles repel each other; two unlike poles attract each other.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnets always stick to things and pull each other together — pushing apart is a special trick you only get with strong magnets.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every everyday encounter with a magnet is an attraction: fridge magnets, magnetic catches, picking up paperclips. Repulsion is only felt when a student deliberately turns one magnet round.
misconceptions.correction: Whether the force is a push or a pull depends only on which poles face each other. Like poles (N–N or S–S) repel; unlike poles (N–S) attract. Both are equally normal magnetic behaviour.

misconceptions.question: Do two magnets have to touch to exert a force on each other?
misconceptions.correct: No. Attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact force.
misconceptions.misconception: The magnets have to reach each other before anything happens — the force only starts at the moment they meet.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most forces a student has met push or pull through contact, and the magnetic force is only obvious in the last centimetre or two, so it looks as though contact starts it.
misconceptions.correction: The force acts across the gap. Bring two north poles slowly together and the push is felt before they meet, growing as the distance falls. That is what makes it a non-contact force.

misconceptions.question: Can an induced magnet be repelled by the magnet that induced it?
misconceptions.correct: No. Induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction.
misconceptions.misconception: If you bring a north pole up to an iron nail, the nail is induced as a north pole, so the two norths should push apart.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly learn that like poles repel, then apply it to induction without asking which way round the poles are induced.
misconceptions.correction: The material is always induced with the unlike pole facing the magnet, so the result is always attraction. The specification is absolute here: induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction, and the force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction.

misconceptions.question: After a paperclip has been picked up by a magnet, is it a magnet from then on?
misconceptions.correct: No. When removed from the magnetic field an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly.
misconceptions.misconception: Once something has been magnetised by a magnet it stays magnetic — that is how a magnet passes its magnetism on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A chain of paperclips hanging from a magnet looks like each clip has been turned into a magnet, and steel objects that have been stroked with a magnet do keep a little magnetism.
misconceptions.correction: The clips are induced magnets: they are only magnetic while they sit in the magnet's field. Take the magnet away and the chain falls apart, because an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly. Only a permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field.

misconceptions.question: Will a magnet attract any metal object?
misconceptions.correct: No. The magnetic materials named by the specification are iron, steel, cobalt and nickel.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnets stick to metal, so a magnet will attract copper, aluminium, brass — anything metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule 'magnets stick to metal, not to plastic or wood' works for almost every classroom object, because most of the metal objects in a classroom are steel.
misconceptions.correction: Only iron, steel, cobalt and nickel are magnetic materials. A magnet will not attract a copper coin or an aluminium can, even though both are metals.

misconceptions.question: Where is a magnet's field strongest?
misconceptions.correct: The field is strongest at the poles of the magnet.
misconceptions.misconception: The middle of the magnet is the strongest part, because that is where all the magnetism is stored and where the bar is at its thickest.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Strongest in the middle' matches everyday ideas about the centre of an object being the heart of it, and a bar magnet looks uniform, so nothing on it marks the ends out.
misconceptions.correction: The poles are by definition the places where the magnetic forces are strongest, and they are at the ends. Hold a paperclip against the middle of a bar magnet and it barely holds; hold it at an end and it grips.

misconceptions.question: Is there a magnetic field in the spaces between the drawn field lines?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The field is the whole region around the magnet where a force acts; the lines are only a way of drawing it.
misconceptions.misconception: The field lines are the field, so between two lines, or outside the last line drawn, there is nothing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Iron filings gather into visible strands with visible gaps, and every textbook diagram shows a fixed number of separate lines, which makes the lines look like real objects.
misconceptions.correction: Field lines are a model. The field exists everywhere around the magnet and fades gradually with distance rather than stopping at an edge. How closely the lines are drawn is the code for how strong the field is: close together means strong.

misconceptions.question: Which way round do the arrows on magnetic field lines go?
misconceptions.correct: The direction of a magnetic field line is from the north (seeking) pole of a magnet to the south (seeking) pole of the magnet.
misconceptions.misconception: The arrows point towards the north pole, because north is the pole that does the attracting.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate north with the 'main' or 'positive' end of a magnet, and arrows are often read as pointing to where something is heading rather than away from where it starts.
misconceptions.correction: Outside the magnet the lines run from north to south. It follows from the definition of field direction: a free north pole placed near the magnet's north pole would be pushed away from it and towards the south pole.

misconceptions.question: Whose force defines the direction of a magnetic field at a point?
misconceptions.correct: The direction of the force that would act on another north pole placed at that point.
misconceptions.misconception: It is the direction a south pole would be pushed, or just the direction the nearest pole lies in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The convention is arbitrary from the student's point of view, so there is nothing to hold it in place unless it is tied to the north-to-south rule for field lines.
misconceptions.correction: The convention is fixed: field direction is the direction of the force on another north pole placed at that point. A south pole would be pushed the opposite way, so using it would reverse every arrow.

misconceptions.question: What is the needle of a magnetic compass made of?
misconceptions.correct: A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet.
misconceptions.misconception: The needle is just a light piece of iron that swings round to line up, the way a paperclip lines up near a magnet.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The needle is small, grey and metallic, and induced magnetism does make iron line up in a field, so the wrong explanation still predicts the right movement in some situations.
misconceptions.correction: The needle is a small bar magnet with its own north and south pole. That is why it settles pointing one specific way rather than either way round: the field turns its north pole in a definite direction.

misconceptions.question: Why does a compass needle swing round and settle?
misconceptions.correct: Because the needle is a small magnet and it lines up with the Earth's magnetic field.
misconceptions.misconception: The Earth's gravity, or the spin of the Earth, drags the needle round until it settles.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gravity and rotation are the two things students already know the Earth does to objects, so they are reached for first when the Earth is said to affect something.
misconceptions.correction: Gravity pulls the needle down, not round, and it would act on any needle, magnetised or not. Only a magnetic field can turn a magnet, so the compass shows that the Earth has a magnetic field.

misconceptions.question: Can iron filings be used to find the direction of a magnetic field?
misconceptions.correct: No. Filings show the shape of the pattern, but a compass is needed for the direction.
misconceptions.misconception: Sprinkling iron filings gives you the whole field, so you can just draw arrows along the lines they make.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The filing pattern is far more striking than a compass plot and appears instantly, so it looks like the complete answer.
misconceptions.correction: Each filing becomes an induced magnet and lines up along the field, but it has no arrow: a filing pointing along a line looks the same either way round. The specification asks for the pattern to be plotted with a compass, whose needle gives the direction as well as the line.

misconceptions.question: What shape are the field lines around a bar magnet?
misconceptions.correct: Smooth curves that leave the north pole and loop round to the south pole, closest together at the poles.
misconceptions.misconception: You draw straight lines from the north pole across to the south pole, evenly spaced, like the rungs of a ladder.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Straight lines are quicker to draw, and students who see the lines as a way of joining the two poles rather than as a map of the field see no reason for them to bend or bunch.
misconceptions.correction: The pattern must show how strength and direction change from one point to another: lines curve outwards from the north pole and round into the south pole, and they crowd together near the poles where the field is strongest, spreading out where it is weaker.

misconceptions.question: Is the north pole of a magnet stronger than the south pole?
misconceptions.correct: No. Both poles are places where the magnetic forces are strongest.
misconceptions.misconception: North is the working end of a magnet — it is the one that attracts and the one the field comes out of, so it must be the stronger pole.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Field lines are drawn leaving the north pole, and the north pole is always named first, both of which make north look like the active end.
misconceptions.correction: The two poles of a magnet are equally strong. A paperclip is held just as firmly at the south end as at the north, and the lines that leave the north pole are exactly the ones that enter the south pole.

misconceptions.question: Is a magnet's field the same strength all the way round it?
misconceptions.correct: No. The strength of the magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet, and it is strongest at the poles.
misconceptions.misconception: A magnet has one strength, so anywhere in its field the force is the same, and outside its range there is none at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Magnets are described in everyday language as 'strong' or 'weak' as if strength were a single property of the object rather than something that varies from point to point.
misconceptions.correction: Field strength is a property of each point in the field. It falls as the distance from the magnet increases, and it is greatest at the poles, which is why field lines are drawn closest together there.

misconceptions.question: What does a compass tell us about the inside of the Earth?
misconceptions.correct: That the Earth produces a magnetic field of its own, which is evidence that its core must be magnetic.
misconceptions.misconception: The needle is responding to magnetic rocks in the ground nearby, so it says nothing at all about the core.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know some rocks are magnetic, and a local explanation feels safer than claiming something about a part of the Earth nobody has ever seen.
misconceptions.correction: Surface rocks vary from place to place, so they could not turn every compass on Earth the same consistent way. A field that acts over the whole planet must be produced deep inside it, which is the evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic.

mcqs.stem: The north pole of one bar magnet is brought close to the north pole of another. What happens?

options.text: They attract each other, because magnets attract
options.rationale: A student whose experience of magnets is all sticking and picking up assumes every magnet pair pulls together.

options.text: Nothing happens until the magnets are touching
options.rationale: Treats the magnetic force as a contact force that only begins when the two magnets meet.

options.text: They repel only if one magnet is much stronger
options.rationale: Gets the repulsion right but makes it conditional on strength; the direction of the force depends only on which poles face each other.

options.text: They repel each other, because the poles are alike
options.rationale: Two like poles repel each other, so two north poles push apart.

mcqs.stem: Why is the repulsion between two north poles described as a non-contact force?

options.text: The magnets touch each other, then spring apart
options.rationale: The student believes contact is needed to start the force, and invents a brief touch to explain the push.

options.text: The push is really an attraction seen in reverse
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe magnets only ever attract and so must reinterpret repulsion as something else.

options.text: The force acts through air but not through solids
options.rationale: Confuses 'not touching' with 'travelling through air'; the magnetic force acts through solid materials too.

options.text: The magnets push apart without ever touching
options.rationale: A non-contact force acts between objects that are not touching, which is exactly what happens as the two north poles are brought together.

mcqs.stem: Where on a bar magnet are the magnetic forces strongest?

options.text: In the middle, exactly midway between the poles
options.rationale: The idea that the centre of the bar is where the magnetism is concentrated is a common and stubborn one.

options.text: At the two poles, at the ends of the magnet
options.rationale: The poles of a magnet are, by definition, the places where the magnetic forces are strongest.

options.text: At the north pole only, not at the south pole
options.rationale: Field lines are drawn leaving the north pole, which makes north look like the stronger, active end.

options.text: Everywhere along the magnet, the force is equal
options.rationale: Treats strength as one fixed property of the whole magnet rather than something that varies from point to point.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes a permanent magnet?

options.text: It produces its own magnetic field at all times
options.rationale: The specification's definition: a permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field, with no other magnet needed.

options.text: It becomes magnetic only when another magnet is near
options.rationale: This describes an induced magnet; students who blur the two pick the definition they met most recently.

options.text: It is any metal, since all metals produce fields
options.rationale: Follows from the belief that magnetism is a property of metal in general.

options.text: It is any object that a magnet is able to pick up
options.rationale: Confuses being magnetic with being attracted; a paperclip is picked up but is not a permanent magnet.

mcqs.stem: A steel paperclip hangs from one pole of a bar magnet. The magnet is then taken away. What happens to the paperclip's magnetism?

options.text: It loses most or all of its magnetism quickly
options.rationale: The clip was an induced magnet, and an induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly once out of the field.

options.text: It stays a magnet permanently from then on
options.rationale: Students think magnetism has been passed on for good, which is why chains of paperclips seem to prove it.

options.text: It loses its magnetism only when it is heated
options.rationale: Same belief in lasting magnetism, with heating imported from other topics as the way to undo it.

options.text: It keeps its magnetism and now repels other iron
options.rationale: Combines lasting induced magnetism with the idea that induction can produce repulsion.

mcqs.stem: What is the key difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet?

options.text: Only the induced magnet is able to lose its magnetism
options.rationale: True as far as it goes, but it is not the defining difference, and students who choose it have not grasped the source of the field.

options.text: Only the induced magnet can both attract and repel
options.rationale: Reverses the actual rule: induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction.

options.text: Only the permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field
options.rationale: A permanent magnet produces its own field; an induced magnet is only a magnet while it sits in someone else's field.

options.text: Only the permanent magnet can be made out of steel
options.rationale: Steel appears in both roles, so the material is not what separates them.

mcqs.stem: The north pole of a bar magnet is held close to an unmagnetised iron nail. What force acts on the nail?

options.text: Repulsion, because the nail is induced as a north pole
options.rationale: Applies the like-poles-repel rule to induction without checking which pole is actually induced.

options.text: Attraction, because induced magnetism always attracts
options.rationale: The nail becomes an induced magnet, and induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction.

options.text: None at all, until the nail has been magnetised
options.rationale: Assumes an unmagnetised object is inert, missing that the field induces magnetism in the iron.

options.text: Repulsion, then attraction once the nail turns round
options.rationale: Imports the way a free magnet swings round before being attracted, which does not apply to induced magnetism.

mcqs.stem: Which list contains only magnetic materials?

options.text: Iron, copper, cobalt and nickel
options.rationale: Copper is a familiar metal, and students who think all metals are magnetic let it through.

options.text: Iron, steel, cobalt and nickel
options.rationale: These are the four magnetic materials named in the specification.

options.text: Iron, steel, aluminium and nickel
options.rationale: Aluminium looks and feels like the metals a magnet does attract, so it is a common false positive.

options.text: Steel, cobalt, tin and copper
options.rationale: Two genuine magnetic materials are used to make the list look right, trapping students who check only the first item or two.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the magnetic field of a magnet?

options.text: The region where it exerts a force on magnetic materials
options.rationale: The field is the region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.

options.text: The set of lines that have been drawn around the magnet
options.rationale: Mistakes the model for the thing: the lines are a way of representing the field, not the field itself.

options.text: The region right at the centre of the magnet only
options.rationale: Locates the magnetism inside the middle of the bar rather than in the space around it.

options.text: The area another magnet must touch to feel a force
options.rationale: Keeps contact in the definition, which is exactly what a field removes the need for.

mcqs.stem: A bar magnet is brought close to a piece of unmagnetised cobalt. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The north pole attracts it, the south repels it
options.rationale: Applies the like/unlike pole rule to a material that has no poles of its own until the field induces them.

options.text: Neither pole affects it until it is magnetised
options.rationale: Assumes only magnets can be acted on, forgetting that cobalt is a magnetic material.

options.text: Both poles repel it, since it has no poles yet
options.rationale: Reasons that an unmagnetised object cannot be attracted, and jumps to the opposite conclusion instead of no force.

options.text: Both poles of the magnet attract the cobalt
options.rationale: The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction, whichever pole is used.

mcqs.stem: A plotting compass is moved from close to a bar magnet to much further away. What happens to the strength of the field at the compass?

options.text: It gets weaker as the compass moves away
options.rationale: The strength of the magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet, falling as the distance increases.

options.text: It stays the same all round the magnet
options.rationale: Treats 'strength' as one fixed property of the magnet rather than of each point in the field.

options.text: It falls to zero outside the drawn lines
options.rationale: Takes the edge of the diagram as the edge of the field, so the field is thought to stop rather than fade.

options.text: It gets stronger as the compass moves away
options.rationale: Reverses the relationship, sometimes from the idea that the force needs room to build up over a distance.

mcqs.stem: On a correctly drawn field pattern of a bar magnet, where are the field lines closest together?

options.text: Near the middle, where the magnet is thickest
options.rationale: Follows from believing the centre of the bar is the strongest part of the magnet.

options.text: Far from the magnet, where the field is weaker
options.rationale: Reads the spacing backwards, or treats the lines as decoration with no meaning attached to spacing.

options.text: Near the poles, where the field is strongest
options.rationale: Line spacing codes for field strength, and the field is strongest at the poles.

options.text: Evenly spaced, since the field does not change
options.rationale: Matches the ladder-of-straight-lines picture, in which spacing carries no information at all.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the magnetic field lines of a bar magnet is correct?

options.text: They are drawn from the south pole to the north pole
options.rationale: Students who think north is the attracting end draw the arrows as though everything heads towards it.

options.text: They point the way a south pole would be pushed
options.rationale: Uses the wrong test pole, which reverses every arrow on the diagram.

options.text: They run in straight lines between the two poles
options.rationale: Describes shape rather than direction, and the shape given is wrong: the lines curve.

options.text: They are drawn from the north pole to the south pole
options.rationale: The direction of a magnetic field line is from the north (seeking) pole of the magnet to the south (seeking) pole.

mcqs.stem: How is the direction of a magnetic field at a point defined?

options.text: By the force that would act on a south pole there
options.rationale: The convention is arbitrary to a student, so the wrong pole is easily substituted.

options.text: By where the drawn lines are closest together
options.rationale: Confuses the code for strength with the code for direction.

options.text: By the force that would act on a north pole there
options.rationale: The specification defines field direction as the direction of the force that would act on another north pole placed at that point.

options.text: By the way the magnet itself would move if free
options.rationale: Describes what a magnet in the field does, not the definition of the direction at a point.

mcqs.stem: What does a magnetic compass contain?

options.text: A small piece of unmagnetised iron
options.rationale: Students who see the needle as ordinary metal explain its movement by induction alone.

options.text: A small bar magnet on a free pivot
options.rationale: A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet, which is why it lines up with a field rather than merely being attracted.

options.text: A small piece of copper on a pivot
options.rationale: Any metal will do, if you believe all metals respond to magnets.

options.text: A small coil that carries a current
options.rationale: Imports electromagnetism into a purely magnetic instrument; a compass needs no power supply.

mcqs.stem: Well away from any other magnet, a compass needle always settles pointing the same way. What does this show?

options.text: The needle is pulled round by the Earth's gravity
options.rationale: Gravity is the effect of the Earth students know best, but it pulls down rather than round.

options.text: The needle is not a magnet, it simply lines up
options.rationale: If the needle were plain iron it could not settle one way round rather than the other.

options.text: The Earth produces a magnetic field of its own
options.rationale: Only a magnetic field can turn a magnet, so a consistent direction shows the Earth has a magnetic field.

options.text: The needle always turns to face the nearest metal
options.rationale: A local explanation cannot account for the same direction being found everywhere on Earth.

mcqs.stem: A student is asked to plot the magnetic field pattern of a bar magnet using a plotting compass. Which method is correct?

options.text: Sprinkle iron filings over the magnet and draw arrows along the lines they form
options.rationale: Filings show the shape of the pattern but carry no direction, so the arrows would be guesswork.

options.text: Draw a straight line from the north pole across to the south pole of the magnet
options.rationale: Produces a diagram from an idea of what a field should look like instead of from measurement.

options.text: Place the compass at one point beside the magnet and record its direction only
options.rationale: One reading gives the direction at a single point, not a pattern that shows how the field changes.

options.text: Mark a dot at each end of the needle, move the compass on to the last dot and repeat
options.rationale: Stepping the compass along, dot by dot, builds a line of the field that can then be joined into a smooth arrowed curve.

mcqs.stem: Which features must a correctly drawn field pattern for a bar magnet show?

options.text: Evenly spaced lines all round, each with an arrow on it
options.rationale: Gets the direction right but throws away the information that spacing carries about strength.

options.text: Curved lines with arrows running from south pole to north
options.rationale: The shape is right but every arrow is reversed.

options.text: Curved lines with arrows, packed closest at the poles
options.rationale: Spacing shows how the strength changes and the arrows show how the direction changes from point to point.

options.text: Straight lines joining the two poles, spaced equally apart
options.rationale: The ladder picture: wrong shape and no indication of changing strength.

mcqs.stem: How is the behaviour of a magnetic compass evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic?

options.text: A compass points to the magnetic rocks in the ground below
options.rationale: A local source cannot explain why compasses everywhere settle in a consistent direction.

options.text: A compass lines up with a field produced inside the Earth
options.rationale: The needle is a magnet, so only a magnetic field can turn it; a field acting over the whole planet must come from within it.

options.text: A compass is pulled towards the North Pole by gravity there
options.rationale: Gravity acts on every object regardless of magnetism, and acts downwards, not sideways.

options.text: A compass turns because the Earth spins, dragging the needle
options.rationale: Rotation would affect any pivoted needle equally, magnetised or not, so it explains nothing.

mcqs.stem: Two bar magnets are placed end to end and pull towards each other. What must be true of the facing poles?

options.text: They are unlike: one north and one south
options.rationale: Two unlike poles attract each other, so an attraction between two magnets means the facing poles are unlike.

options.text: They are alike, because like poles attract
options.rationale: Reverses the rule; often chosen by students who think 'the same' means 'goes together'.

options.text: One is a magnet, one an induced south pole
options.rationale: Assumes every attraction must be induction, but the question states both objects are bar magnets.

options.text: Both must be south poles facing each other
options.rationale: Picks a specific like-pole pairing, chosen by students who believe south is the passive, attracting end.
